options: Count components as edges arrive one by one
Find the edge that closes a cycle

problems.title: Redundant edge
hints: The first union whose endpoints share a root.
problems.solution: After [1, 2], [2, 3], [3, 4], nodes 1 and 4 are already connected, so [1, 4] closes the cycle.

problems.title: Why both optimisations?

parts.prompt: With neither path compression nor union by size, the worst case per find is…

problems.solution: Linking a chain gives O(n); size-balanced trees have depth ≤ log₂ n; adding compression gives the inverse-Ackermann bound.

problems.title: MST

parts.prompt: Minimum total cost to connect all points?

hints: Prim from (0, 0): its cheapest link is to (2, 2) at 4.

problems.title: Cut property

options: The cheapest edge crossing any cut is in some MST; Kruskal's edge is the cheapest crossing the cut between its endpoints' components

hints: Exchange: swap it into any MST that lacks it.
problems.solution: If an MST omitted that edge, adding it creates a cycle that crosses the cut again through an edge at least as expensive; swapping gives a spanning tree no worse.

problems.title: Choose Kruskal or Prim
problems.statement: n = 10⁴ points in the plane, all pairs as candidate edges.

options: Array Prim, O(n²) time and O(n) memory

problems.solution: About 50M edges: storing and sorting them is heavy. Array Prim never materialises them.

problems.title: Reverse time
problems.statement: Edges are removed one at a time; after each removal, report the number of components.

options: Process the removals in reverse as additions, starting from the final graph, then reverse the answers

problems.solution: Offline reversal turns deletions into unions. It's the same move as "process the constraints in the right order".
